Check catalog (K1–K8)
IDcheckwhat it measures
K1FK verificationHand position from the retargeted joint angles + link lengths vs the scaled human hand target (cm).
K2Joint position limitsShare of frames where any raw joint angle is beyond its limit; which joints.
K3Joint velocity limitsPer-joint angular velocity vs the actuator's max velocity.
K4Clamping distortionHand position difference between the raw and the clamped (position + velocity limited) trajectory.
K5Reach envelopeMonte Carlo workspace of waist + arm; frames where the scaled human hand target is outside it.
K6Foot slidingPlanted-foot runs of the MB-Lab retarget whose ankle drifts more than a threshold.
K7Self-collision proxyForearm/hand capsules vs the torso capsule on the executed (clamped) motion.
K8JitterHigh-frequency (above the cutoff) RMS noise in the joint angles.

5. Reach envelope

Envelope: 300,000 samples per arm over waist + arm joint limits (Beta(½,½) sampling to populate the extremes); a target is "inside" if a sample lies within 3.0 cm.

6. Retargeting method comparison

methodmean FK error (cm)max FK error (cm)clamped FK error (cm)frames past a limit
ik_refined1.673.084.3933%
joint_angle12.4418.1813.5929%

FK error = distance from the robot tool point (forward kinematics of the joint angles) to the human hand position scaled by arm length. Joint-angle-only copies the human's joint rotations, so link-length differences move the hand; IK moves the arm joints (damped least squares, regularised toward the joint-angle solution) until the hand lands on the target.

7. What this means for data collection

  1. Only 50% of the analysed frames are executable as demonstrated. Of 11 clips, 0 are usable as is, 6 need clamping and 5 are not feasible for this robot. Raw human demonstrations should never go into training un-audited.
  2. Violations concentrate in a few joints: r_shoulder_yaw (7% of frames), r_wrist_yaw (7% of frames), head_pitch (6% of frames). Those are the joints to watch in demonstration review, and the first candidates for a hardware or protocol change.
  3. Reach is a task-design problem. The worst reach case is cmu_69_73 (walk up, lean over, pick up an object, set it down elsewhere): 20% of frames have a hand target outside the robot's workspace. Protocol fix: mark a reach zone on the table or shelf and have operators keep objects inside it.
  4. Motion type predicts feasibility. Mean share of frames past a position limit by task type: overhead_reach 97%, bend_pick 60%, messy 34%, squat_pick 26%, pick_place 15%, carry 12%, manipulation 10%, reach 1%. Task types at the top of that list are where human range exceeds the robot's, so they are the ones to design around (different object placement, a different robot, or exclude from training).
  5. Speed matters as much as range. cmu_14_01 has 52% of frames above a joint velocity limit. Clamping a fast demonstration makes the robot lag it, which moves where the hand ends up (K4: up to 16.3 cm mean). An operator pacing guideline is the first protocol change to try; this run does not test whether it works.

8. Methodology and limitations

Pipeline

  1. Mocap → MB-Lab. CMU BVH (Y-up, 120 Hz, frame 0 = T-pose) is parsed, converted once to Blender axes (Z-up, faces −Y) and decimated to 30 Hz. For each mapped bone the source world rotation delta from its T-pose is applied to the target bone's T-pose reference orientation (the MB-Lab A-pose bone swung onto the source T-pose direction), never a raw rotation copy. Root motion is the hip-joint midpoint's displacement scaled by the leg-length ratio. Baked to an action in Blender 4.0.2 with MB-Lab 1.8.1.
  2. MB-Lab → robot. Segment rotations are expressed in the robot frame and decomposed onto the robot's signed joint axes (exact Euler for 3-DoF joints with temporal continuity, tracked least squares for the 1–2 DoF joints), parent first. The pelvis supplies the heading; the 2-DoF waist absorbs trunk tilt. Optional IK refines each arm to the scaled human hand position.
  3. Raw vs clamped. Raw ignores limits (what the human did). Clamped clips each joint to its position limits and slew-limits it to its max velocity (what the robot can do).
  4. Checks K1–K8 with thresholds from config/thresholds.yaml; the verdict rules are in the same file.

Limitations

  • The robot is a generic, hand-specified skeleton; its limits, velocities and link lengths are not any real robot's. Treat verdict percentages as demonstrations of the method.
  • Collision is a capsule proxy (forearm/hand vs one torso capsule); no head, legs, or arm-to-arm checks.
  • The waist has no roll DoF and wrists have no roll, so those components of the human motion are least-squares dropped; this shows up in K1 for joint-angle-only retargeting.
  • Foot sliding (K6) is measured on the MB-Lab retarget (the human side); the robot's feet are not planted by an IK solver. No balance/dynamics model: legs are only checked against joint and velocity limits.
  • Rotation retargeting does not match end-effector positions across body proportions; that is what the IK stage is for. Hand/finger motion is not retargeted.
  • Mocap comes from one public dataset (CMU, a few subjects); the clips are short windows, not a representative demonstration set.
